title: `RelaxedServiceNameValidation` feature gate does not cover ingress `spec.defaultBackend`
body:
### What happened?

The `RelaxedServiceNameValidation` feature gate implementation in `allowRelaxedServiceNameValidation()` might be incomplete. It checks service names in `spec.rules` but does not check `spec.defaultBackend.service.name`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go#L701

This creates inconsistent behavior: Ingresses with relaxed service names in rules can be updated, but those with relaxed names only in defaultBackend cannot.


### What did you expect to happen?

The feature gate should consistently handle relaxed service name validation for both `spec.rules` and `spec.defaultBackend`. When the feature gate is disabled, existing Ingresses with RFC 1123-compliant but RFC 1035-noncompliant service names (e.g., "1-default-service") should remain updatable regardless of whether those names appear in `rules` or `defaultBackend`.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate
2. Create Ingress with defaultBackend with a service name starting with a digit
3. Disable RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate
4. Attempt to update this Ingress
5. The update fails because the old service name starts with a digit.

### Anything else we need to know?

I found a minor typo in comment: "old Ingresss" should be "old Ingress"
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go#L710

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy namespace lookup raced newly created namespaces, produces spurious "namespace not found" rejections
body:
### What happened?

When creating new workload (observed with Deployment and StatefulSet) immediately after creating its namespace, there is a possibility that watch case has not yet caught up to the new namespace existing.

Naively, this would result in frequent failures, but apiserver guards against this by falling back to live client when namespace was `NotFound`. Example: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ab3e83f73424a18f298a0050440af92d2d7c4720/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/predicates/namespace/matcher.go#L88

The issue happens infrequently but can be forced by overriding informer lister to always return NotFound for a specific namespace (see repro instructions below). This way, the call to informer's lister would always fail, while the call to client would remain unaffected - this would force the fallback path, ensuring it is present.

### What did you expect to happen?

No 404 errors when creating StatefulSets in existing namespaces - even immediately after ns creation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?



```
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
@@ -20,7 +20,6 @@ package v1

 import (
        corev1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
-       errors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        labels "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels"
        listers "k8s.io/client-go/listers"
        cache "k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache"
@@ -47,17 +46,3 @@ type namespaceLister struct {
 func NewNamespaceLister(indexer cache.Indexer) NamespaceLister {
        return &namespaceLister{listers.New[*corev1.Namespace](indexer, corev1.Resource("namespace"))}
 }
-
-// Get retrieves the Namespace from the index for a given name.
-// Objects returned here must be treated as read-only.
-// This method overrides the embedded Get to add custom logic.
-func (nl *namespaceLister) Get(name string) (*corev1.Namespace, error) {
-       // 1. Check if the requested namespace is "lalala"
-       if name == "lalala" {
-               // 2. Return not found error if it is
-               return nil, errors.NewNotFound(corev1.Resource("namespace"), name)
-       }
-       // 3. Otherwise, use the parent implementation from the embedded ResourceIndexer
-       return nl.ResourceIndexer.Get(name)
-}
-
```


Steps to reproduce:

  1. Apply the diff above to apiserver code.
  2. Set up a cluster using that apiserver.
  3. Create the namespace "lalala"
  4. Create a StatefulSet in that namespace
  5. Observe the request failing with 404 - it should succeed despite the damaged lister code

### Anything else we need to know?

Based on our (limited) set of observations, we believe the regression happened between 1.32 and 1.33

How do we know what character encoding a container uses for its stdout / stderr?

Given the [question](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135292#issuecomment-3539709957), and until we either:

> How do we know what character encoding a container uses for its stdout / stderr?

Currently it is hard coded to [text/plain](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d450ef773127374148abad4daaf28dac6cb2625/pkg/registry/core/pod/rest/log.go#L109) for all containers, irrespective of what they may or may not be setting. This results in this bug where container generating utf-8 charset are forced rendered using `text/plain`.  

The [fix](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135293) replaces existing `text/plain` to `text/plain; charset=utf-8`, this already is better than simple `text/plain`, but then that fix also allows us to respect other mime types if the container has set them (e.g. `text/plain; charset=latin-1`)

If the container happens to emit UTF-8, great. The client can switch from a heuristic to certainty.

### What happened?

When a Deployment is referenced by multiple Services, the associated RemoteEndpoints are sometimes not deleted when the Deployment or Pods are terminated. This leads to the presence of stale RemoteEndpoints in the system.

This issue is observed only in large-scale environments with a high number of Services and Endpoints, suggesting a potential race condition or delayed cleanup in the controller logic.

nodes.title: kube-proxy/winkernel: fix stale RemoteEndpoints due to premature clearing of terminatedEndpoints map
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The winkernel proxier maintains a map of terminated endpoints that is updated
in `endpointsMapChange()`. This information is used to delete the remote endpoints after the required loadbalancers are updated/deleted. When multiple Services are updated in batch during a
single `syncProxyRules()` call, `endpointsMapChange()` is invoked multiple times.
Each invocation currently clears the `terminatedEndpoints `map, causing data from
previous updates to be lost.

This results in incomplete cleanup and stale RemoteEndpoints when Deployments
are referenced by multiple Services at large scale.

**Fix**
Move the `clearTerminatedEndpointsMap()` invocation to occur before:

```
_ = proxier.svcPortMap.Update(proxier.serviceChanges)
_ = proxier.endpointsMap.Update(proxier.endpointsChanges)
```

This ensures the map is cleared only once at the beginning of `syncProxyRules()`
and remains valid throughout the update process.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #135144

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
- Reproducible on large AKS clusters using Windows kube-proxy.
- Tested with multiple Services referencing the same Deployment.
- Verified that stale RemoteEndpoints no longer persist after Deployment deletion.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fix Windows kube-proxy (winkernel) issue where stale RemoteEndpoints remained
when a Deployment was referenced by multiple Services due to premature clearing
of the terminatedEndpoints map.
```

```
geomean                                                                                                          81.00                         195.0        +130.82%
```

Yeah, the change is definitely the cause here.

I'm trying to think of ways to address this. So as far as I can tell, there are two ways we can handle this:

1. Determine which pools are incomplete before we start converting them, which allows us to just throw away any slices in the pool that doesn't target the node. The benefit is that we don't have to do any conversion or other handling of those slices, but the drawback is the work needed to determine if the pools are incomplete up front. This is what was implemented in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134466. 

2. The other option is to keep enough state as part of the current loop through the slices so we can determine later if a pool is incomplete. The drawback here is that we need to do this for every pool in the cluster, since we can't know if a pool is relevant for a node without looking at every slice. So in situations where there are a pool per node, we need to keep track of completeness for every pool. I have a quick-and-dirty attempt at this approach in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...mortent:DRAPerfImprovement. I haven't run the full perf suite on it, but it seems to have the same performance problems as the merged PR.

This actually becomes an even larger issue for Partitionable Devices. Since we are scoping the counter sets to a pool, the allocator needs to know about all allocated devices that consumes counters in that pool, meaning we need to know about allocated devices on other nodes than the current one.

I'm wondering if an option here is to say that all ResourceSlices in a pool must have the same node selector? The resourceslice-controller kinda already enforces this since it only allows specifying the NodeSelector on the Pool level:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/afb2b97425317948e9e59b2a7871fca5bbb2ab08/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/resourceslice/resourceslicecontroller.go#L128-L153

For `PerDeviceNodeSelection` things gets a bit more complicated, but we could still require that all slices in the pool use the same node selector. This would allow the allocator to throw away slices that doesn't target the current node, knowing that no slices in the pool will target the node and therefore we don't care about whether the slice is complete. But it can't be validated on admission and validating it in the allocator would be expensive.

Both https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135056 and  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135056 fix this based on the idea from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135032#issuecomment-3476686304, but the latter is a bit simpler and has more test cases.

title: Kube-proxy(IPVS) v1.31.0 fails to add KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entry for hairpin traffic, causing SNAT failure
body:
### What happened? **Kubernetes version** : `registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.31.0` We are running a minimal two-node cluster set up with `kubeadm`: one control-plane node (Ubuntu) and one worker node (Debian). When a Pod tries to connect to a Service (ClusterIP), the connection behavior depends entirely on the client's location: - **Cross-node access (Works):** Connections from the control-plane node to the Service IP (`10.104.26.46`) succeed. - **Same-node access (Fails):** When a client Pod (`10.244.0.103`) tries to connect to the Service IP, and the backing Pod (`10.244.0.71`) is scheduled on the _same worker node_, the connection fails. The cluster is running `kube-proxy` in **`ipvs` mode**. **Evidence:** 1. **`tcpdump`** on the node shows the client Pod (`10.244.0.103`) sends a `[SYN]` to the Service IP (`10.104.26.46`). This packet is correctly DNATed to the server Pod IP (`10.244.0.71`). 2. The server Pod (`.71`) replies with a `[SYN, ACK]` directly to the client Pod (`.103`). 3. The client Pod (`.103`) immediately sends a `[RST]` because it received a reply from an unexpected IP (`.71`) instead of the Service IP (`.46`) it initiated the connection with. _This confirms a **SNAT failure** for the hairpin traffic._ 4. In `ipvs` mode, `kube-proxy` still relies on `iptables` and `ipset` for hairpin SNAT. The `iptables` rules in `KUBE-POSTROUTING` correctly point to an `ipset` named `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` to handle this: ```bash root@CZDebian1:~# iptables-save -t nat ... -A KUBE-POSTROUTING -m comment --comment "Kubernetes endpoints dst ip:port, source ip for solving hairpin purpose" -m set --match-set KUBE-LOOP-BACK dst,dst,src -j MASQUERADE ... ``` 5. However, checking the `ipset` reveals that `kube-proxy` **fails to add the required entry** for the client/server Pod pair: ```bash # ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK | grep 10.244.0.71 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.71 # The required (dst-ip, dst-port, src-ip) rule is missing, # expected missing entry: 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.103 ``` Crucially, when manually adding the correct entry for debugging, the connection is temporarily fixed. ```bash # ipset add KUBE-LOOP-BACK 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110 # At this point, the connection from ...110 works ``` However, within seconds, kube-proxy's reconciliation loop runs, compares the state to its (incorrect) "expected state", and actively deletes the manually added entry, calling it "legacy". This proves its internal logic is flawed. ```bash # kube-proxy logs show: I1025 14:07:28.276446 1 ipset.go:174] "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry from ip set" ipSetEntry="10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.103" ipSet="KUBE-LOOP-BACK" I1025 14:08:26.203177 1 ipset.go:174] "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry from ip set" ipSetEntry="10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110" ipSet="KUBE-LOOP-BACK" ``` ### What did you expect to happen? `kube-proxy` should correctly identify that the client Pod (`.103` / `.110`) and the server Pod (`.71`) are on the same node. It should then **create and persist** the required SNAT rule in the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` `ipset` (e.g., `10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110`). It should _not_ delete manually added, correct entries, as this indicates a flaw in its reconciliation logic. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Set up a minimal Kubernetes cluster (e.g., v1.31.0) using `kubeadm` with one control-plane node and one worker node. 2. Configure `kube-proxy` to run in `ipvs` mode (e.g., by patching the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap or during `kubeadm init` via the `KubeProxyConfiguration`). 3. Ensure the `kube-proxy` configuration uses the default `iptables.masqueradeAll: false`. 4. Deploy a server application (e.g., `nginx` or `mysql`) and expose it via a ClusterIP Service. 5. Using a `nodeSelector` or `nodeName`, ensure this server pod (**`Pod-Server`**) is scheduled and running on the **worker node**. 6. Deploy two client/debug pods using an image that includes `netcat`, such as `nicolaka/netshoot:latest`: * Schedule one pod (**`Pod-Client-A`**) onto the **worker node** (the same node as `Pod-Server`). * Schedule the other pod (**`Pod-Client-B`**) onto the **control-plane node**. 7. **Test cross-node connection (baseline):** * Exec into `Pod-Client-B` (on the control-plane) and connect to the server's ClusterIP: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Result:** The connection **SUCCEEDS**, as expected. 8. **Test same-node (hairpin) connection (the bug):** * Exec into `Pod-Client-A` (on the worker node) and connect to the *same* ClusterIP: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Actual Result:** The connection **FAILS** (e.g., times out). 9. **Investigate on the worker node:** * SSH into the **worker node** (where `Pod-Server` and `Pod-Client-A` are running). * Run `ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK`. * **Observation:** The set is missing the required entry for this connection. An entry for `,tcp:,` does not exist (though an entry for pod-to-self, `,tcp:,`, may exist). 10. **Apply manual fix:** * On the **worker node**, manually add the missing `ipset` entry: ```bash ipset add KUBE-LOOP-BACK ,tcp:, ``` 11. **Verify manual fix:** * Immediately re-run the test from `Pod-Client-A`: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Result:** The connection **SUCCEEDS** immediately. 12. **Confirm `kube-proxy` rollback:** * Wait for the `kube-proxy` sync interval (e.g., \~30-60 seconds). * Check the `kube-proxy` pod logs on the worker node, observing messages about ipset changes (e.g., "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry"). * Run `ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK` again on the worker node. * **Result:** The manually added entry has been removed by `kube-proxy`, and the connection from `Pod-Client-A` will begin failing again. ### Anything else we need to know? This appears to be a bug in `kube-proxy`'s logic, as all related configurations have been verified as correct: - **`kubelet` Config:** `hairpinMode: "hairpin-veth"` - **`kube-proxy` Pod Args:** `command: --hostname-override=$(NODE_NAME)` and `env: NODE_NAME: (v1:spec.nodeName)` - **`kube-proxy` ConfigMap:** `mode: "ipvs"`, `clusterCIDR: "10.244.0.0/16"` - **`Node` Object:** `PodCIDR: 10.244.0.0/24` (and both Pods are in this CIDR) - **Client `Pod` Object:** `spec.nodeName` correctly matches the node name (`czdebian1`) - **`Service` Object:** `internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` **Workaround:** The only workaround found was to edit the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap and set **`iptables.masqueradeAll: true`**. This bypasses the broken `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` logic by SNAT-ing _all_ Pod traffic, which incidentally covers the hairpin case. This confirms the bug is specific to the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` ipset population logic when `masqueradeAll` is false. ### Kubernetes version
```console root@CZHomeServer:~# kubectl version Client Version: v1.31.0 Kustomize Version: v5.4.2 Server Version: v1.31.0 ```
### Cloud provider
Build a kubeadm cluster locally, one worker node and one control plane node
### OS version
```console # On Linux: $ cat /etc/os-release root@CZHomeServer:~# cat /etc/os-release PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS" NAME="Ubuntu" VERSION_ID="22.04" VERSION="22.04.4 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)" VERSION_CODENAME=jammy ID=ubuntu ID_LIKE=debian HOME_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/" SUPPORT_URL="https://help.ubuntu.com/" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/" PRIVACY_POLICY_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/legal/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy" UBUNTU_CODENAME=jammyu $ uname -a root@CZHomeServer:~# uname -a Linux CZHomeServer 6.8.0-85-generic #85~22.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Fri Sep 19 16:18:59 UTC 2 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux root@CZDebian1:~# cat /etc/os-release PRETTY_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)" NAME="Debian GNU/Linux" VERSION_ID="12" VERSION="12 (bookworm)" VERSION_CODENAME=bookworm ID=debian HOME_URL="https://www.debian.org/" SUPPORT_URL="https://www.debian.org/support" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.debian.org/" root@CZDebian1:~# uname -a Linux CZDebian1 6.1.0-37-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.1.140-1 (2025-05-22) x86_64 GNU/Linux ```
### Install tools

This is an excellent bug report with comprehensive analysis. I've encountered similar IPVS hairpin traffic issues in production environments. Based on the detailed investigation, this appears to be a logic flaw in the kube-proxy's IPVS reconciliation loop when determining which client-server Pod pairs require KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entries.

## Technical Analysis

The root cause is in kube-proxy's `proxier.syncIPSetEntries()` method where it builds the expected state for the KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset. The logic incorrectly evaluates same-node Pod-to-Service traffic patterns, specifically:

1. **Missing Entry Generation**: The algorithm fails to recognize when a client Pod and server Pod are co-located on the same node and need hairpin SNAT
2. **Incorrect State Reconciliation**: The "legacy entry" deletion confirms the reconciler believes the manually-added correct entry shouldn't exist
3. **Node Locality Detection**: The issue likely stems from improper node name/IP correlation during endpoint enumeration

## Proposed Solutions

### Immediate Fix
The bug is likely in `pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go` in the `syncIPSetEntries` function. The logic for determining same-node relationships between client and server endpoints needs investigation around:

```go
// Pseudo-code location of likely bug
for _, ep := range endpoints {
    if shouldAddLoopBackEntry(clientNodeName, ep.NodeName) {
        // This condition is likely failing
    }
}
```

### Code Areas to Investigate
1. **proxier.go:syncIPSetEntries()** - Primary suspect for missing entry generation
2. **endpointsInfo node tracking** - Verify proper node name propagation from kubelet
3. **IPVS service topology awareness** - Ensure same-node detection logic is sound

### Testing Strategy
I recommend adding unit tests specifically for:
- Same-node client/server endpoint scenarios
- KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entry generation logic
- Edge cases with multiple Pods per node

This impacts production clusters significantly as hairpin traffic is common in microservices architectures. The workaround of `masqueradeAll: true` works but introduces unnecessary SNAT overhead for all traffic.

**Priority**: High - affects core networking functionality in IPVS mode
**Impact**: Service mesh, multi-tenant clusters, and dense Pod deployments

I'd be happy to investigate the exact code paths and provide a patch if maintainers can confirm this analysis aligns with the expected behavior.

You need to do `sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1`.

kubeadm used to do this itself, but that was wrong because most plugins don't need it (and don't want it; it slightly reduces network throughput), and besides, the network plugins that _do_ need it ought to set it themselves rather than expect the user's cluster-deployment tool to have done it.

Flannel apparently currently documents the fact that you need to load the `br-netfilter` kernel module (which is true), and checks for that at startup (by seeing if the `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables` sysctl exists), but it _doesn't_ document the fact that that sysctl needs to be set to `1`.

I'm going to add a comment to https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/issues/2068.
@czczcz831 can you confirm that setting the sysctl fixes it?

Hi @danwinship, thanks very much! 

`sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1` immediately fixed the issue.

I just have one follow-up question regarding my original analysis: Is the current behavior of `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` (only containing server-pod-ip,port,server-pod-ip) actually the expected design?

I originally suspected it was a bug because the set didn't contain an entry for the client pod (server-ip,port,client-ip). Does enabling the sysctl mean that kube-proxy is not required to maintain specific client-server pair entries in the ipset to handle this traffic correctly?

Yes, `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` is only supposed to have entries for self-to-self.

The issue in both cases is that if a packet gets DNATted on the outbound path, we have to make sure that its reply path takes it somewhere where it will get un-DNATted before it gets back to the client pod.

kube-proxy breaks that into two cases:
- If the client pod and the server pod are _the same pod_, then if kube-proxy were to DNAT the pod and not masquerade it, then it would end up getting sent back to the pod with the source and destination IP both set to the pod's IP, so when the pod replied, it would try to send the reply directly to itself, and then fail. So to prevent that from happening, kube-proxy masquerades the packet as well, so now when the pod receives it, it thinks the packet came from the node IP, not from itself, so it sends the reply back out to the node, and then it gets un-DNATted and un-masqueraded and then routed back to the pod. This is what `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` is for.
- If the client pod and the server pod are _different pods_, then kube-proxy assumes that the reply from the server to the client will come back out to the host network namespace, and the DNAT will get undone there, so everything will just work. But if the client and server are on a bridge, and that bridge _doesn't_ have `bridge-nf-call-iptables` set, then the reply packet will just immediately go from the server to the client without letting iptables/conntrack un-DNAT it first, causing your problem. Setting `bridge-nf-call-iptables` fixes it, by making the bridge properly un-DNAT the reply packet before passing it on to the client.

Hacking `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` the way you did works around the problem by just causing _all_ local packets to get masqueraded, so then even in the "different pods" case, the reply packet has to get sent all way back off the bridge to the host network namespace. But it's inefficient because (a) you're making the return packet path longer, and (b) you're making the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` set bigger.

### What happened?

When creating a ResourceClaim with 2 requests with 2 different device class that have a config, the config reported in the allocation devices status is not mentioning from which request the config is coming from.       - opaque:

Ok this has lead to nasty downtime for me. They are called stateful sets for a reason: they contain stateful data and now the entire state of the system had to be rebuilt from. the ground up. 1.34 has been available since august already, I don't understand how it took that long before anybody experienced this problem.

> They are called stateful sets for a reason: they contain stateful data and now the entire state of the system had to be rebuilt from. the ground up.

The stateful part is in the persistent volumes, and the stable identity of pods in the set, which were not impacted by this issue.

A rollout of a new revision of a statefulset replaces those individual pods, and could cause _disruption_ for applications which are sensitive to any pod in the set restarting or being replaced, but should not break stateful data...  if you are seeing state problems after a no-op rollout, I think that means _any_ upgrade of your nodes (which replaces pods) or _any_ update of your statefulset image or pod spec (which would roll out new pods) would have caused similar loss.

title: when resuming a suspended kubernetes job, unhandled error of job controller occured in the log of kube-controller-manager pod
body:
### What happened? try to resume a suspended job, there are repeated error logs: error="syncing job: tracking status: adding uncounted pods to status: Job.batch is invalid: status.startTime: Required value: startTime cannot be removed for unsuspended job" as shown in the attached image. ### What did you expect to happen? no error occur in log of kube-controller-manager pod ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Create a kubernetes job. The job starts to run. 2. Suspend the job. The job is suspended. kubectl patch job/myjob --type=strategic --patch '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}' 3. Resume the job. kubectl patch job/myjob --type=strategic --patch '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}' The commands to suspend / resume job are from the offical doc：https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#suspending-a-job ### Anything else we need to know? https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/batch/validation/validation.go#L699-L705 Doubt if it is caused by !ptr.Equal(oldJob.Status.StartTime, job.Status.StartTime). when resume the job, job.Status.StartTime becomes current time which is differenent from oldJob.Status.StartTime although job.Status.startTime is not nil. Interesting.

I also see this for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134629
cc @dejanzele @mimowo @tenzen-y
I am able to reproduce this on k8s 1.33.1 also.

Looks like this was added by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/e568a77a931a1cf4239a4a5fa43e2b05bad3abdf.

cc @mimowo 

When I did my testing I didn't see any functional issues with this though. Job still suspends and resumes.

Oh yes, this is a bug because when resuming the Job the Job controller would always update the status.startTime: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1058

To fix this I can see two options:
1. allow to update status.StartTime for unsuspended jobs
2. allow to update status.startTime for unsuspended jobs only when Job is resumed (so that isUpdated=true): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1047-L1048

I would suggest going for (2.) to be more strict.

cc @tenzen-y @atiratree @soltysh wdyt?
I already spoke with @mimowo , I'll look into it as part of the managed-by graduation to stable.
Wouldn't it be better if we set `.status.startTime` to nil every time `.spec.suspend` is set to true in the apiserver update logic? Or do you expect this to break anything?
I suppose we could also nil it a bit later in the controller when updating the `Suspended` condition to `True/JobSuspended`

Let me add for context that users of Kueue don't face this issue because Kueue clears status.startTime during the "stopJob" procedure: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/blob/main/pkg/controller/jobs/job/job_controller.go#L184-L192

> Wouldn't it be better if we set .status.startTime to nil every time .spec.suspend is set to true in the apiserver update logic? Or do you expect this to break anything?

This sounds like a good idea if this was written on day one, but since this is an old code of Job controller, I'm more tempted to adjust the new validation logic. 

IIRC it was considered some time ago, but we weren't sure about race conditions when user wants to quickly suspend / unsuspend. However, I don't see any catastrophic case anyway this is what we do in Kueue currently.

> I suppose we could also nil it a bit later in the controller when updating the Suspended condition to True/JobSuspended

^ should happen after the pods get deleted, but I guess a race can occur there as well. So to conclude we are weighing a race against a stricter Job API validation.

I guess we could also consider disabling setting suspend to true unless `True/JobSuspended` is observed, but that also seems limiting/problematic with existing clients.

> > I suppose we could also nil it a bit later in the controller when updating the Suspended condition to True/JobSuspended
> 
> ^ should happen after the pods get deleted, but I guess a race can occur there as well. So to conclude we are weighing a race against a stricter Job API validation.

I definitely agree there is room for improvement, but this is also touching a long existing behavior, so risky as a quick fix. 

So, I would rather consider introducing a new condition like `JobFullySuspended` to mark that all Pods are deleted.

Yeah, the "safe" path forward I see is: 
1. relax validation as a bugfix just when Resuming (option 2) from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134521#issuecomment-3414248956
2. consider improvements for "sequenced/strict" suspension, but that could be a separate "suspendMode: strict" maybe.  Then we could wait with validations until the suspention completes (pods are deleted, JobFullySuspended is reached, and startTime is cleared), before allowing to resume, but this would be a separate KEP likely with low ROI  because orchestrators like Kueue already do it.

> Yeah, the "safe" path forward I see is:
> 
> 1. relax validation as a bugfix just when Resuming (option 2) from [when resuming a suspended kubernetes job, unhandled error of job controller occured in the log of kube-controller-manager pod #134521 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134521#issuecomment-3414248956)
> 2. consider improvements for "sequenced/strict" suspension, but that could be a separate "suspendMode: strict" maybe.  Then we could wait with validations until the suspention completes (pods are deleted, JobFullySuspended is reached, and startTime is cleared), before allowing to resume, but this would be a separate KEP likely with low ROI  because orchestrators like Kueue already do it.

IIUC, the above status validations were introduced to provide guide for external Job controllers leveraging managedBy field.
So, I'm ok with relaxing the validations with `allow to update status.startTime for unsuspended jobs only when Job is resumed (so that isUpdated=true):`.

As a long-term effort, we might want to introduce the processing state as a sibling of SuccessCriteriaMet and FailureTarget.
But, yes a long-term solution should be part of another KEP (issue).

> 1. relax validation as a bugfix just when Resuming (option 2) from [when resuming a suspended kubernetes job, unhandled error of job controller occured in the log of kube-controller-manager pod #134521 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134521#issuecomment-3414248956)

I'm even inclined to relax it such that it's allowed to clear the value when job is suspended.

title: No share ID in DRA kubelet plugin's API
body:
### What happened?

kubelet plugin API does not support ShareID information. The ShareID is an additional identifier to the device name which may be generated by DRAConsumableCapacity feature ( that is introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5104). 

The DRA driver which refers to this API for preparing resource needs to pass ShareID to CDI spec's device ID. Otherwise, the same node will fail to create a container according to the duplicate ID. 



### What did you expect to happen?

Pods can be successfully created when sharing the same device with DRAConsumableCapacity.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable DRAConsumableCapacity feature, Enable DRA driver with allowMultipleAllocations device, Create two pods allocating the same device.

### Anything else we need to know?

Without the change to k/k, a driver can have a workaround which wrap the plugin API appending with shareID and use it as a PreparedDevice.

From 
```go
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
to
```go
type DRADevice struct {
	drapbv1.Device
	shareID *types.UID
}
type PreparedDevice struct {
	Device         DRADevice
	ContainerEdits *cdiapi.ContainerEdits
}
```
implemented code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/939b1fdd3e3efec3a3c7ea758c394c5aabdfa422

However, it looks cleaner when we do that in the provided API.
The change needs at driver is only extending the CDI id with share id if not nil: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver/commit/4a625314cb46ed38018d05e17a397420335277eb.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The Kubelet's DRA manager was failing to report device health status in a pod's status for certain types of resource claims. The logic incorrectly assumed that the claim name used within the container's spec (`container.resources.claims[*].name`) was the same as the metadata name of the actual ResourceClaim object.

This assumption is false in two key scenarios:
1.  When a claim is generated from a `ResourceClaimTemplate`, Kubernetes creates a `ResourceClaim` object with a randomized suffix in its name.
2.  When a user defines a pre-existing claim in `pod.spec.resourceClaims`, they can provide a local name that differs from the actual `ResourceClaim` object's name.

In both cases, the code would fail to find the claim's information in its internal cache, resulting in the health status not being populated, as reported in issue #134482.

This fix corrects the logic by using `pod.Status.ResourceClaimStatuses` as the authoritative map to look up the actual, generated name of the `ResourceClaim` object. This ensures that both templated and renamed claims are resolved correctly before their health status is retrieved from the cache.

Additionally, this change introduces a new dra manage unit tests that specifically covers templated and renamed claims to prevent future regressions.

title: Asynchronous preemption can be initiated even before the previous one is finished for the same pod
body:
### What happened?

In the asynchronous preemption, the preemptor is blocked in PreEnqueue until API calls are made to delete the victims. However, it doesn't wait for the last victim to be deleted not to cause a race condition (in which we could ignore the Pod/Delete event).

This means that when API calls take longer (e.g., due to throttling), the pod may start the preemption process for that last pod again, even if the previous one hasn't finished. Each preemption process would create a Pod/Delete API call to delete the last victim. As a result, kube-scheduler can create dozens of API calls to preempt a single pod.

Normally, we should have multiple safeguards to avoid such tight loops, but currently, all of them can be bypassed:
- The pod waits in unschedulablePods and must be woken up by some event. However, when there are many preemptions going on in the cluster, some unrelated Pod/Delete events can wake up such a pod.
- Even after being woken up, the pod should go to backoffQ and wait for the backoff penalty. However, we have a Pop from backoffQ feature that, if activeQ is empty, pop these pods from backoffQ directly, ignoring the backoff penalty.
- Synchronous API calls to update the status of a pod when it cannot be scheduled also worked like a kind of barrier, limiting the performance of the scheduler (the number of cycles per second) and making it dependent on the processing performance of the kube-apiserver. In this scenario, such behavior was beneficial, because kube-scheduler wasn't able to retry one pod that quickly. This call has been replaced by an asynchronous version by Asynchronous API calls feature.

/sig scheduling
/kind regression

### What did you expect to happen?

Kube-scheduler shouldn't start the preemption process for a pod until the previous one is finished. At least, such behavior should be minimized.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use scheduler_perf `PreemptionBasic` benchmark, with smaller # of pods and nodes (to reduce the testing time), e.g.
```yaml

    featureGates:
      # Choose one to disable:

      # SchedulerAsyncPreemption: false
      # SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ: false
```

> Normally, we should have multiple safeguards to avoid such tight loops, but currently, all of them can be bypassed:

b) Disable PopFromBackoffQ, as it creates a shortcut for preemptor pods, bypassing one of the safeguards.
c) Disabling AsyncAPICalls, which indirectly caused this problem in v1.34, due to the replacement of the synchronous pod status patch API call with its asynchronous version.

### Anything else we need to know?

Currently I am suspecting that the crash is related to this specific line which appears in the crash dump:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/csi/csi_attacher.go#L255

```
klog.V(4).Info(log("attacher.GetDeviceMountPath(%v)", spec))
```
***
1. `log()` function calls `fmt.Sprintf()` to format the `spec` parameter
2. `spec` is a `*volume.Spec` containing a PersistentVolume object
3. `PersistentVolume.String()` method is called (generated protobuf code)
4. This calls `PersistentVolumeStatus.String()` which includes:
   go
  LastPhaseTransitionTime: + strings.Replace(fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime), "Time", "v1.Time", 1) + ,,

5. LastPhaseTransitionTime is a *metav1.Time (pointer to metav1.Time)
6. When fmt.Sprintf("%v", this.LastPhaseTransitionTime)
 is called on a nil pointer, Go attempts to call the String() method
7. metav1.Time embeds time.Time, and time.Time.String() has a value receiver: func (t Time) String()

8. To call this method, Go tries to dereference the nil *metav1.Time pointer, causing a panic

**Windows-specific behavior:**
- fmt.Sprintf normally recovers from panics during string formatting
- However, on Windows with compiler optimizations enabled, sometimes this panic recovery fails
- The panic escalates to runtime.sigpanic and eventually runtime.throw
- **Workaround:** Changing the log statement to print spec.Name instead of the full spec
 object avoids the crash

**Evidence supporting this theory:**
1. Crash disappears with compiler optimizations disabled (-gcflags="-N -l"
)
2. Crash disappears when avoiding the problematic `klog.V(4).Info` call on `spec` and switching to `spec.Name()`
3. Stack trace shows runtime.sigpanic failing to recover properly on Windows
4. Issue is reproducible and consistently tied to CSI volume reconstruction logging

This suggests a bug in Go's Windows runtime where panic recovery during string formatting fails, causing what should be a recoverable panic to become a fatal crash.

I am not sure if this is a known issue in Windows. However, I think a way to fix this is to implement a `String()` method of v1.Time that does an explicit null check, so that we do not have to rely on golangs default sigpanic recovery (which seems to not work well in Windows environments). title: Kubelet rejects pod with "NodeAffinity failed" due to stale informer data
body:
#### What happened

This issue is similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/100467 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/92067.

We have a controller that adds labels to a node after it starts up. It looks like there are cases where the scheduler is able to see the new node labels and schedule a pod, but the kubelet somehow doesn't see the new labels - it has stale data in its informer cache. Whatever the reason for the stale data, the result is that the kubelet rejects the pod with "NodeAffinity failed".

#### What did you expect to happen

Kubelet to be able to detect the new node labels and not reject the pod. 

The only reason that we need to keep the node affinity / node selector check in the kubelet is in case someone sets `nodeName` directly on the pod, so that it does not go through the scheduler, so we can't just remove enforcement on the node level.

The short-term fix would be for the kubelet to synchronously fetch the node object when (and only when) it sees these "NodeAffinity failed" errors and try again. To ensure we do not introduce additional heavy traffic when there many pods being scheduled at once, we will have to keep a new cache, separate from the informer cache. The logic would be like:
- Read the node object from the informer
- If we get a NodeAffinity failed error, read the node object from our new cache
- If we still get a NodeAffinity failed error, fetch the node object synchronously from the api server
The cache should be updated whenever we see a node object that is newer than the one we are currently storing - this can come from either the informer or from the synchronous fetch. 

Long term, maybe we can re-consider the flow for `nodeName`, or leverage something like [kubelet synchronous admission](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O9rDeYhGWMbtg-DQmhqKvNsQSHWJSwvSEeNpXTKMvZg/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.6ggs708p6vvu) to keep the scheduler and kubelet coordinated. There are also some more general discussions about what to do when informer data is stale, maybe the outcomes there can help here.

#### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

You'd probably have to restart kubelet a whole bunch of times, and have a controller that modifies the node labels whenever it restarts.

#### Environment
- Kubernetes version: The issue is reported as persistent from versions v1.18-v1.28+, and it is unlikely that it has been fixed in a more recent version.
- Cloud provider: GKE

/assign
/cc @tallclair

```go
	cachedNode *v1.Node
	client clientset.Interface
}

func (c *nodeCache) GetCache() *v1.Node {
	informerNode, _ := c.nodeLister.Get(c.nodeName)
	if c.cachedNode == nil || isNewer(informerNode, c.cachedNode) {
		return informerNode
	}
	return c.cachedNode
}

func (c *nodeCache) GetSync (*v1.Node, error) {
	node, err := c.client.CoreV1().Nodes().Get(context.Background(), c.nodeName, metav1.GetOptions{})
	if err != nil { return nil, err }
	c.cachedNode = node
	return node, nil
}
```

I'm just not sure how to do the `isNewer` check. I thought we weren't supposed to parse resourceVersion, but it looks like the [scheduler does it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bbd859808d0cef566fbfc89639926b7cc50d9bd5/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L236), so ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Then the steps look like:
1. Run the admission check using the node from `GetCache`
2. If there is a node affinity error, rerun the admission check using the node from `GetSync`

My preferred solution would be to just drop the affinity check from the Kubelet, but I don't think there's a backward compatible way we can do that. IMO the affinity check should just be a scheduling policy. Once the pod is scheduled to the node, the Kubelet shouldn't need to enforce it.

> My preferred solution would be to just drop the affinity check from the Kubelet, but I don't think there's a backward compatible way we can do that.

Yeah I'm not sure I understand what the affinity check in the kubelet is for. If someone is setting `nodeName` explicitly to bypass the scheduler, I could see the desired behavior as being to ignore node affinity (what is the purpose of setting `nodeName` to a node that's just going to reject the pod?). But I agree that it is too late to change this now.

> I'm just not sure how to do the `isNewer` check. I thought we weren't supposed to parse resourceVersion, but it looks like the [scheduler does it](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bbd859808d0cef566fbfc89639926b7cc50d9bd5/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L236), so ¯_(ツ)_/¯

There's agreement on relaxing to let clients start comparing... specifics proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5505

> My preferred solution would be to just drop the affinity check from the Kubelet, but I don't think there's a backward compatible way we can do that.

Yeah, historically labels/selectors and taints/tolerations have been used not only as scheduling directives but also as protection boundaries in combination with admission forcing / forbidding pods from selecting / tolerating specific nodes, so Kubelet also doing a check to refuse to run pods assigned to it but not matching its labels / tolerating its taints is something we can't drop.

nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

If the informer cache is stale, it is possible for kubelet to reject a node with `NodeAffinity failed` errors after a pod is scheduled to it. More details are in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133997.

This PR updates kubelet to implement a node cache interface. When the admit handlers run into a node affinity issue, the kubelet will now synchronously fetch the node from the api server, update its internal cache accordingly, and try again.

2 commits:
1. A tiny simplification of `getNodeAnyway` - I dug into the history a bit and found that this function was written the way it is because there _used_ to be polling in `GetNode` that we wanted to avoid, but that polling no longer exists.
2. Update the predicate admit handler to use the new node caching methods to fetch the node synchronously on admission failure and try again.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133997

T=0.1s: The container's command runs, creates the /work/first_run_done file, and exits with code 1. The container is now in a Terminated state. T=0.1s to T=5s: The probe worker is still waiting for its initial delay to expire. It has not run a single probe. T=5s: The worker's delay is over, and it runs doProbe for the first time. It sees that the container is Terminated. The onHold flag is false because a probe has never completed. It proceeds to the check: if c.State.Running == nil. This is true. It executes the faulty return logic: return c.State.Terminated == nil || w.pod.Spec.RestartPolicy != v1.RestartPolicyNever. Since the pod's RestartPolicy is Never, this evaluates to false, and the probe worker terminates itself. Meanwhile: `kubelet` sees the terminated init container and, honoring its restartPolicy: Always, starts a new instance of it. The syncloop will attempt to recreate the probe. However due to the bug in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go#L194 , the loop will `return` early because the main container's probe already exists, it fails to check the initContainer's probe. Result: The new container instance starts, but its probe worker is gone. No new worker is created. The Kubelet sees a running container with a startup probe but not have a successful ran, assuming it's not ready. The main-container never starts. ### What did you expect to happen? startupProbe should honor the container's restartPolicy. The startupProbe should continue to probe even if the sidecar container has failed initially and restarts. Running as a sidecar." sleep infinity fi startupProbe: # This delay MUST be long enough for the first container instance # to start, run its command, and terminate. initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 2 failureThreshold: 3 # The probe command itself is irrelevant, as it will never be run # by the first worker. exec: command: ["/bin/true"] containers: - name: main-container image: registry.k8s.io/pause # Added a startupProbe to the main container. startupProbe: initialDelaySeconds: 5 periodSeconds: 5 exec: command: ["/bin/true"] ``` ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version

nodes.title: Fix startup probe worker termination for sidecar containers
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Fixes a bug where startup probe workers terminate incorrectly for sidecar containers with `restartPolicy=Always` when the pod has `restartPolicy=Never`. This causes main containers to remain stuck in "Initializing" state even after sidecar containers successfully restart.

**Problem Description:**
- Pod with `restartPolicy: Never` 
- Sidecar container with `restartPolicy: Always` and startup probe
- Sidecar fails initially, then restarts successfully
- **Bug**: Main container never starts (stuck in Initializing)
- **Root cause**: Probe worker terminates based only on pod restart policy

**Solution:**
Minimal fix adds container-level restart policy check **only for init containers** to the probe worker continuation logic, allowing workers to continue for sidecar containers while preserving existing behavior for regular containers.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #132826

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- **Minimal change**: Single line addition with proper null safety checks and init container validation
- **No breaking changes**: Existing behavior preserved for regular containers  
- **Scoped to init containers only**: Fix only applies to restartable init containers (sidecars)
- **Comprehensive testing**: Unit tests cover both sidecar and regular container scenarios
- **E2E test included**: Validates end-to-end functionality

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a startup probe race condition that caused main containers to remain stuck in "Initializing" state when sidecar containers with startup probes failed initially but succeeded on restart in pods with restartPolicy=Never.
```

title: Deletion of csi-node-plugin Pod causes driver entry to be removed from CSINode object; kube-scheduler schedules more than driver's allocatable
body:
### What happened?

With @plkokanov we hit in our environments the following issue multiple times:
```
% k -n shoot--foo--bar describe po etcd-main-0

Events:
  Type     Reason              Age                 From                     Message
  ----     ------              ----                ----                     -------
  Warning  FailedAttachVolume  35s (x47 over 80m)  attachdetach-controller  AttachVolume.Attach failed for volume "pv-shoot--shik--shak-1234" : rpc error: code = Internal desc = Attach volume /subscriptions/<omitted>/resourceGroups/shoot--shik--shak/providers/Microsoft.Compute/disks/pv-shoot--shik--shak-1234 to instance shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 failed with Retriable: false, RetryAfter: 0s, HTTPStatusCode: 409, RawError: {\r
  "error": {\r
    "code": "OperationNotAllowed",\r
    "message": "The maximum number of data disks allowed to be attached to a VM of this size is 16.",\r
    "target": "dataDisks"\r
  }\r
}
```

When we checked, the CSINode object for the corresponding Node was reporting the correct volume attachment limit:
```
% k get csinode shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 -o yaml

spec:
  drivers:
  # ...
  - allocatable:
      count: 16
    name: disk.csi.azure.com
    nodeID: shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5
    topologyKeys:
    - topology.disk.csi.azure.com/zone
    - topology.kubernetes.io/zone
```

According to the Node status and according to the VM state in Azure, it had already 16 disks attached.
```
% k get no shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 -o json | jq '.status.volumesAttached | length'
16

% az vm show -g shoot--shik--shak --name shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5 | jq '.storageProfile.dataDisks | length'
16
```

kube-scheduler wrongly sheduled a Pod with a volume to the `shoot--shik--shak-cpu-worker-etcd-z1-6c956-mhcw5` Node as the Node already had its volume attachments limit reached.

We found that this happens due to csi-node-plugin Pod deletion. On deletion of this Pod, we see that the driver section from the CSINode object is removed and it is added only when the new csi-node-plugin Pod starts.

The corresponding handling in kube-scheduler's NodeVolumeLimits plugin is: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a7242fcff768658019f878cb691583dcbcfefb2d/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi.go#L197-L201

If we fail to fetch the limit from the CSINode object, kube-scheduler let's the Pod to be scheduled.

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-scheduler to do not schedule Pods with volumes to Nodes that already have their volume attachment limit reached.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To reproduce the removal of the driver section after csi-node-plugin Pod deletion:

1. Start watching the CSINode object:
```
 k get csinode "$NODENAME" -w -o yaml > "~/csinode-$NODENAME.yaml"
```

2. In a new terminal window delete the csi-node-plugin Pod

3. Make sure that the CSINode object watch is as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: CSINode
metadata:
  name: node-1
spec:
  drivers:
  - allocatable:
      count: 8
    name: disk.csi.azure.com
    nodeID: node-1
    topologyKeys:
    - topology.disk.csi.azure.com/zone
    - topology.kubernetes.io/zone
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: CSINode
metadata:
  name: node-1
spec:
  drivers: null
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: CSINode
metadata:
  name: node-1
spec:
  drivers:
  - allocatable:
```

title: Overaggressive Routes Controller
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug

**What happened**:
`Route controller` is unnecessary too aggressive. The [current control loop](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/route/route_controller.go#L115) loops through the node list every `10s`. Each node will generate a `GET` call to cloud resource manager (ARM in case of `azure`) to assert the route existence, This quickly burns through the quota afforded to each subscription (the umbrella concept used by `azure` to manage multiple clusters/ resource groups) by the underlaying cloud. Nodes does not change their own ip that frequent on `azure` or any cloud/om-prem deployment for that matter. Once the cluster burns through the quota its control plane will become practically unusable until quota refill, refresh or manual shutdown/start of controller to slow down the calls.

Setting it to higher period is not the best solution, since we need the route controller to kick in in case of scale up/down or the unlikely case of node changing IPs. 

**What you expected to happen**:
`Route Controller` must generate the smallest possible of cloud calls. Ideally, only when needed. And must be reasonably fast in reaction to changing state such as `new nodes`, `deleted nodes`, or changing `node ip`  

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Either run many small clusters (10 X 20 nodes) in the same `azure` subscription (or the equivalent concept on different environments), Or run one large cluster (400++ node). The controller will quickly log `HTTP 429` (in `azure` case) throttling errors 

**Proposed Solution**
change `Route Controller` implementation to `Service Controller` [like](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/service_controller.go#L136) implementation using `shared informer`. Because `node` object gets frequently updated (example node status updates) the controller should maintain an in memory cache of `node:ip` and should only call out the `cloud provider` when the node is new or its ip has changed. We can extend this by a `full sync` every long period just in case of faulty state drifts.

nodes.title: feat(ccm): watch-based route controller reconciliation
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The route controller in the cloud-controller-manager currently operates with a static reconciliation interval. Depending on the scale of the cluster, this can quickly lead to exceeding the rate limits set by cloud providers.

This PR introduces a new watch-based route controller that triggers reconciliation only when a node is added, deleted, or when there are updates to the `Status.Addresses` or `PodCIDR` fields.

Additionally, a new feature gate, `CloudControllerManagerWatchBasedRoutesReconciliation`, is introduced, which is disabled by default.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #60646

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
KEP [5237](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5237) is merged and has status implementable.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Add cloud-controller-manager feature gate CloudControllerManagerWatchBasedRoutesReconciliation
```
